doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: How he came to the balafon and slit drum
summary: Jackie McLean's history class, Abdullah Ibrahim, and Billy Higgins's slit drum led him to collecting balafons.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: And you got into the balafon over the years. What prompted that?

Different work experiences. I spent a little time with Jackie McLean, kind of, so I spent some time with Jackie McLean in the very early 80’s when I first came out of D.C., Jackie brought my brother and I to the University of Hartford and we went to school there for a minute. So Jackie, I took a history class with him where we studied some of the African music, you know, the roots of jazz. So it got me into thinking about a lot of African traditions. Then when I got to New York and I started to work with Betty and then in the meantime of working with Betty I also started doing some gigs with Abdullah Ibrahim. So there, now I’m getting some South African flavor and playing with some of the other great African musicians that he knew. At the same time or a little before that I had met and become very, very good friends with Billy Higgins. We had become like really close where we would share music. If he came to New York he’d come to my house — he’d come in and we’d play drums and play stuff. I’d go to L.A., he’d come get me, go over his house, we’d play, and he would start showing me some of the different instruments that he played. Because Billy could pick up a little bit of everything and play. You know, guitar and stuff. So the first thing he showed me was this little box, we called it a slit drum. It’s like a wooden box. You’ve seen them, they’ve got slabs cut up on the top where they get different notes. So he showed me one of those and I started playing it. Oh yeah. So when you check out some of my first recordings that’s what I’m using, it’s a slit drum. And then it just got me to being curious and every time I’d get to these different cities I’d go to the music stores or I’d be playing on a festival or something — it’d be an African festival so I’d go down and check out some of the instruments. And one day I found a little balafon, a small balafon. And I started playing it. So I said you know what? This would be even easier to carry than a slit drum and I liked the sound. So I started messing around with the balafon. And that’s how that came in.

Sure. Just because the sound, being the way that they’re made and from different tribes and different parts of Africa, all of them are different. So if you’d come by my house I’ve got like almost 10 or 15. I kind of collect them. Because I’ll play them for a while for a different sound and melodies will come out of different ones for me. So I have several of them. Because the tone system and the scales that they use, they’re never the same. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-
